activity.title: A number came out last week that I haven't been able to stop thinking about. Orca Security's 2026 State of AI Security Report, which pulled telemetry from over 1,200 production cloud environments, found that 99.9% of AI vulnerability alerts with an available fix remain unpatched. 81.2% of companies running AI packages have at least one known vulnerability. These aren't theoretical exposures or edge cases. These are known issues, with fixes available, sitting unaddressed across the majority of organizations that have deployed AI into production. The reason isn't negligence. It's prioritization, and 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐨𝐟 𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐤. If your compliance program tells you you're secure because your controls are documented and your last audit was clean, there's no built-in signal telling you to go patch the AI package your engineering team quietly spun up six months ago. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐬𝐤 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫. Organizations are building, deploying, and operating AI in the cloud, but basic cybersecurity hygiene is often being sacrificed for speed. That tradeoff might feel invisible right now. It tends to become very visible very quickly. This is the gap between certified and actually protected, playing out at scale, in real time. #Cybersecurity #AIRisk #RiskManagement #SecurityCompliance #AIGovernance #Research ...more ...more

Hot take: a blockchain-based fintech just had nearly a million customer records stolen. They had a $3.2B valuation. They presumably had audits. They presumably had certifications. Figure, the San Francisco-based lending platform, disclosed earlier this year that hackers made off with personal information on close to one million customers: names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, and email addresses. The company was quick to note that Social Security numbers and financial account details weren't part of it. Which is true. And also a little beside the point. Here's what actually stood out to me: cybersecurity researchers linked the attack to ShinyHunters, a group that's been responsible for some of the largest breaches of the last few years. This wasn't a novel, unpredictable threat. It was a known actor using known methods against a company that, by all appearances, was doing things right. That's the part worth sitting with. Not "how did they get breached" but "what did their risk posture actually look like the day before this happened?" Did their compliance program reflect that exposure? Did anyone own that question? Regulators have been ramping up scrutiny of security practices at digital-first financial companies, and the CFPB has made clear that fintech firms face the same data protection obligations as traditional banks. The enforcement pressure is real. But enforcement pressure drives documentation. It doesn't automatically drive the kind of continuous, operational risk awareness that would have flagged this earlier. This is exactly the pattern I've been researching. Will keep you posted with updates. #RiskManagement #Fintech #Cybersecurity #DataBreach #Compliance #FinancialServices Source: https://lnkd.in/gURdgcTB ...more ...more

🔍 Most companies don't lose control of their risk management on purpose. It happens gradually, usually right around the time they start scaling. I've been digging into this lately: how security and compliance functions evolve as companies grow, particularly around frameworks like SOC 2 and ISO 27001. What's interesting isn't the frameworks themselves, it's what happens to risk management once those frameworks enter the picture. In the early days, risk feels intuitive. A small team knows where the soft spots are because they built the thing. But as companies scale and compliance requirements show up, often driven by a customer deal or an investor requirement, something subtle shifts. Risk management starts getting defined by what the audit checks for, rather than the audit reflecting what the company is actually worried about. The checklist becomes the risk model. That's not a criticism of the frameworks. It's a pretty natural response to growth; you need something standardized once you can't rely on tribal knowledge anymore. But people I've talked with described a real moment of realization: passing an audit and still not feeling like they had a handle on their actual exposure. The certification and the confidence stopped moving together. I'm still working through what makes the difference. More on this soon. #RiskManagement #Cybersecurity #SOC2 #ISO27001 #Compliance #Scaling #MBA #HaasSchoolOfBusiness ...more ...more

Google just dropped Gemini 3 and Nano Banana Pro— and they launched a hackathon in SF to push the limits of both models. I placed 2nd Overall alongside Dhruv Jena , Rohan Dash , and Rishabh Abhishetty . It was an intense industry-style build where we competed and networked with leading tech engineers with 10+ years experience and serial startup founders. We went in with one idea, but midway through the hackathon we realized we wanted to take full advantage of Gemini 3 and especially Nano Banana’s capabilities. That pushed us to pivot halfway and build something completely new: ForenSight AI. ForenSight AI is a forensic analysis platform that takes in real-world evidence (images, video, audio, text), runs it through Gemini 3’s reasoning engine, and produces: - a unified world model of the scene - a timeline of events - contradiction detection analysis across evidence and witness statements - multiple plausible scenarios - a realism suspect sketch - and 4K photorealistic reconstructions using Nano Banana Huge shoutout to Cerebral Valley for organizing the event and the neat venue and big respect to the winners and everyone who shipped something ambitious under a tight deadline. Thank you to the judges and Google DeepMind Team for your time and help. What's next with ForenSight AI: We’re now taking this weekend prototype and shipping it into a full-stack platform — adding deeper functionality, a node-based evidence flow that recommends investigative leads, and a systemized case board. Microsoft, TikTok, ByteDance, American Express, and Capital One all opened Summer 2027 internships today. 225 roles in a single day. If you were not looking today, you missed all of it. TikTok added 161 roles. ByteDance added 51. Microsoft posted SWE, PM, and TPM American Express added 5 Capital One opened all of its Summer 2027 programs You can see all of them here, free, no account needed: https://lnkd.in/gf_rBmdW The problem was never that internships are unavailable. It is that they are scattered across hundreds of company career pages, community spreadsheets, and Discord channels that move too quickly to follow. By the time most students hear about a role, the first wave of applications has already arrived. I know that gap personally. Last cycle I kept finding postings a week after they went up, and a week late means a thousand applications are already ahead of you. Most students did not miss the applications. They missed the moment they opened. So over the past weeks I built Internship Radar 2027. It checks official employer career pages and job APIs on a schedule, removes duplicate listings, and sorts roles by when they actually opened rather than when they were discovered. It now tracks 946 open internships across 220 companies, with nearly 600 added in the past seven days. Three things I would ask, in order of how much they matter: Go look today, not in the fall. Recruiting has already started whether or not it feels like it has. Set an email alert for your roles and locations. It takes about thirty seconds, and it is the difference between hearing about the next launch in the first hour and hearing about it next Thursday. That is the entire reason this exists. Send this to one person who is recruiting this cycle. Most people still do not know what happened today. Still building it every week. Thank you to the 9,000 people who have used it and the 25,000 applications started since launch 3 weeks ago. I did not expect that. If a listing is wrong or a company is missing, hit report. It comes straight to me. Good luck this recruiting cycle. I am genuinely rooting for everyone applying. #Internships #SoftwareEngineering #ProductManagement #CareerDevelopment #Summer2027 #job #career

The AI infrastructure buildout is one of the fastest capital deployment cycles in history. The security programs around it are not keeping up. In 2025 alone, U.S. data center construction starts reached $77.7 billion; a 190% year-over-year increase. In the first half of 2026, another $88 billion in projects are set to break ground. Hyperscalers are moving at a pace the security industry hasn't had to match before. AI data centers are being built faster than they can be secured. And the security challenge isn't just scale, it's structural. These aren't traditional data centers running independent servers. 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐲'𝐫𝐞 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞, 𝐦𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 where a vulnerability in one layer: firmware, network interconnects, multi-tenant isolation, can cascade in ways that a standard risk framework wasn't designed to model. The pattern is familiar. A new capability gets deployed at speed. The risk program tries to catch up. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐩 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬, and in most organizations, that gap is neither measured nor reported. Speed is a competitive advantage until it isn't. The compliance programs that were built for last decade's infrastructure aren't automatically equipped for this one. #Cybersecurity #AIInfrastructure #RiskManagement #DataCenterSecurity #SecurityPosture #Research
